claims.claim: Making a small payment on an old debt does not restart the clock.
claims.quote: but no such payment of itself shall revive a cause of action once barred.
claims.note: This covers an already-barred claim. Before the bar, a payment by the party to be charged on principal or interest due on a promissory note starts a new period. The text has no minimum payment amount.

claims.claim: Signing something on an old debt does not restart the clock.
claims.note: The document's content matters. Section 360 allows a signed writing containing an acknowledgment or promise to serve as evidence of a new or continuing contract.

claims.claim: The limit for an old debt is four years.
claims.quote:
Within four years:
(a) An action upon any contract, obligation or liability founded upon an instrument in writing, except as provided in Section 336a;
claims.note: Section 337 specifies covered actions and exceptions; it does not establish a four-year limit for every old debt.

claims.claim: The four-year limit keeps running no matter what you pay.
claims.note: The promissory-note payment provision expressly stops the running of time and starts a new period for a qualifying payment before the claim is barred.

claims.claim: The four-year limit keeps running no matter what you sign.
claims.note: Section 337(d) expressly allows extension pursuant to section 360, which addresses signed acknowledgments and promises.

claims.claim: You can safely make a payment.
claims.note: The assurance ignores the effect of a qualifying pre-bar payment on a promissory note.

claims.claim: You can safely sign a payment plan.
claims.note: The source gives no such assurance. The plan may contain a signed acknowledgment or promise.

flags.text: The claim that the clock always keeps running conflicts with section 360's new-period rule for qualifying promissory-note payments.
The draft does not distinguish a payment made before the bar from one made afterward, or a signed acknowledgment or promise from other signed documents.
The draft treats all debts as subject to the same four-year period and all payments and signed documents as having the same effect.
“You can safely” directs the reader to act without knowing the debt type, timing, or terms of the writing.
A reader could make a qualifying payment near the deadline or sign an acknowledgment or promise, weakening a limitations defense.

result.summary: The sources support a narrow payment-alone rule for an already-barred claim, not the draft's assurance that paying or signing cannot affect the limitations defense.
